title: Chore Charts by Age (2 to Teen) — Free Printables
meta_description: Chore charts by age, from toddlers to teens. Pick your child's age to get a free, age-appropriate printable plus advice from a dad of four (and foster parent).
intro: A two-year-old "helping" you vacuum and a fifteen-year-old running a babysitting shift are not the same job — so they shouldn't share the same chart. That mismatch is exactly what sends most chore charts to the recycling bin by week two. This is the age-ladder hub: pick your child's age below and you'll land on a chart built for where they actually are, not where you wish they were. I'm Andrew, and in our house we've run chores across the full range — four kids of our own (currently 9 to 18) and three foster children we cared for as toddlers. One thing we learned early: the chart is a tracking tool for us as parents, not a motivation gimmick for the kids. The motivation comes from a simpler idea we say out loud all the time — we all contribute. Use the age picker to get the right starting point, and read on for how those expectations should shift as a kid grows.

sections.heading: How chores should change from toddler to teen
sections.body:
The biggest mistake we see is treating chores as one fixed list. They aren't. They're a ladder, and each rung looks different.

At 2 to 4, it's barely about the house at all — it's self-care. Getting their own clothes on, brushing teeth (we did it alongside them, because little kids want to do what their parents do), cleaning up their own mess. If a toddler wants to 'vacuum' because you are, let them, and teach exactly one small technique. You're building comfort, not getting a clean floor.

Around 4 to 5, we add a little shared responsibility — wiping down a bathroom, a group space. Here's the honest part: don't expect good results. You will redo the work. The point isn't quality yet; it's that they start to feel like part of a family unit with responsibility toward each other.

From 6 to 12, the expectations finally catch up to the ability. Dishes, trash, starting to help cook, and outdoor work. Our son loves shadowing me on house repairs and asks a hundred questions — that turns into real competence over time. Complexity rises as proficiency rises.

Teens are their own animal, and I'll be blunt: the family wall chart stops working around 13. We've raised two teens through it now. What replaced it is in the teen-specific page, but the headline is that it stops being a chart and starts being something closer to a job.

sections.heading: How to pick the right starting point
sections.body:
Start with your child's actual age in the picker above — that gets you a chart that matches their developmental stage. But age is the starting line, not the rule.

If your child is new to chores entirely, or you've had charts fail before, drop down one rung from their age. A 7-year-old who's never had real expectations does better starting on the 6-7 chart with room to grow than getting handed a list they'll quietly ignore. You can always raise the bar; clawing back from overwhelm is harder.

We also learned this acutely as foster parents. The three little ones we cared for came to us at 2 and 3, and for them the structure mattered even more than it did for our own kids. Consistency they could count on — same steps, same order, every day — was something they could trust, and it helped them settle and self-regulate faster than I expected. The lesson generalizes: when in doubt, choose the level your child can succeed at consistently, because predictability is what makes the whole thing stick. Pick the age, watch for a week or two, and adjust up when the current rung gets easy.

sections.heading: The philosophy: a tracking tool, not a sticker economy
sections.body:
Every per-age chart on this site is built on the same belief, so it's worth saying plainly. The chart exists to help you, the parent, see how each kid is doing and decide when to step in. It is not there to bribe the child into cooperating.

That matters because it changes what you reach for when motivation dips. The answer isn't a flashier reward — it's reinforcing the expectation: in our house, everyone contributes, full stop. We deliberately keep rewards and screen time separate from chores. We don't make our kids 'earn' fun by working, and we don't pay per task. Allowance exists, but it's gated on quality, consistency, and attitude over time — not handed over chore by chore like a vending machine.

When you frame chores as a transaction, you teach kids to ask 'what do I get?' When you frame them as membership in a family, they stop asking. The chart just lets you keep honest track of who's pulling their weight, so the conversation can be about contribution instead of negotiation.

faq.q: What chores are appropriate for each age?
faq.a: Roughly: ages 2-4 focus on self-care (dressing, teeth, picking up their own mess). Ages 4-5 add light shared spaces — expect to redo the work. Ages 6-12 take on dishes, trash, cooking help, and outdoor jobs as their skill grows. Teens shift to bigger, job-like responsibilities. Each per-age chart above is built specifically for that band, so pick your child's age to see the actual list rather than guessing.

faq.q: What age should kids start doing chores?
faq.a: You can start as young as 2 to 3, but at that age it's really self-care and letting them 'help' without requiring it — you're building comfort, not productivity. Real assigned chores that you track tend to land around 4 to 5, when kids can grasp that they're part of a family unit with responsibilities. In our house that's also when allowance enters the picture, modestly and tied to attitude and consistency.

faq.q: Should I pick the chart by my child's age or their ability?
faq.a: Start with age, then adjust for ability. The age picker gives you a developmentally appropriate baseline. But if your child is brand new to chores or past charts have failed, start one rung lower so they can succeed consistently, then raise the bar as it gets easy. We found predictability matters more than ambition — a level they can hit every day beats an impressive list they ignore.
